 © 2026 Yahoo. All rights reserved. "Madden," the long-awaited John Madden biopic, would have been better served if it had promoted itself as a comedy from the beginning.
 Nicolas Cage puts on a fat suit and some prosthetics to play the legendary Oakland Raiders coach, groundbreaking NFL color commentator and the man who put his name behind one of the most popular and successful video games of all time. But the suspension of belief achieved when an actor fully embodies and immerses themselves in a role to the point where you forget they're playing a character did not happen in this 110-minute film. You know it's Cage the whole time because his portrayal of Madden came with the acclaimed actor's legendary, unmistakable voice, accent and mannerisms.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The film begins with a few documentary-style solo cutaways that are needlessly interspersed throughout the movie. They feature Madden, Raiders owner and Madden's best friend Al Davis, played more successfully by Christian Bale, and Madden's loving wife Virginia, played well by Kathryn Hahn, who's running out of patience in their marriage. The Raiders are 0-5 in AFC championship games under Madden, and Virginia tells him that if they beat the rival Pittsburgh Steelers, he needs to come home to spend more time with his family. Madden, Davis and the Raiders arrive at the Oakland Coliseum for the game, and so does Shane Gillis for some reason as a late cast addition , playing a superstitious neighbor named Vince McGary who brings chicken feet and other good luck charms to the game.
 Nicolas Cage, left, and Riko Shibata arrive at the premiere of "Madden" on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, at The Culver Theater in Culver City, Calif.
 (AP Photo/Richard Shotwell) Madden can't stop thinking about football and diagramming plays, and the film hammers home this point by putting them on screen far too many times. While the game play in the film is mediocre, the old-timey yellow score graphics were a nice touch as the movie quickly speeds through the Raiders' two wins over the Steelers and Vikings as Madden and Davis get nervous, banter with one another and celebrate their championship with as many f-bombs as possible. The salty language is solely why this movie is rated R and not PG-13. 
 As the Raiders celebrate their first title, Madden brings out a birthday cake for Virginia that started out as loving x's and o's but quickly devolved into another diagrammed play. Gillis' McGary is brought into the locker room to celebrate, and a video game creator named Trip Hawkins, who created Electronic Arts and eventually makes the Madden video game, first introduces himself to the head coach somehow at the Super Bowl postgame press conference. John Mulaney played Hawkins yet didn't mention the movie once when he hosted "Saturday Night Live" this past weekend, continuing a theme of Amazon, which produced the movie, not wanting to promote the film too much and backing away from a previously planned wide theatrical release.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Madden and Davis are inseparable even after the championship, yelling plays at each other and rationalizing how Madden hasn't seen his family in months to the point where he forgets how old his two sons are. Madden starts complaining about his stomach pain, which Davis says can be cured with saltines and Tums, specifically the peppermint kind. It turns out to be a stomach ulcer that forces Madden into retirement from the Raiders, but not before several jokes about vomiting and gas. A serious and dramatic biopic, this is not.
 Madden is insufferable as a retired stay-at-home dad, going to see Steve Martin's "The Jerk" several times, hanging with McGary and explaining plays out loud to his dog. Davis convinces Madden to take a meeting with CBS for a color commentator job, which Madden reluctantly accepts despite calling their NFL broadcast team "haircuts." The film then successfully chronicles Madden's rise as a household television superstar, introducing his Madden cruiser bus and fear of flying, his catchphrases and commercials for Miller and Tinactin, the Thanksgiving turducken, his love of food and his pioneering use of the telestrator. 
 This sets up an absurd and unrealistic scene where Davis and Hawkins are fighting over Madden's future. Davis wants Madden to come back and consult after a terrible 1987 season and Hawkins wants Madden to give over his beloved five-pound playbook to educate the masses for EA. There's a car chase scene and a ridiculous moment where Davis, who moved the Raiders to Los Angeles, tries explaining the rap group NWA to Madden, who questions whether Dr. Dre actually received a medical degree. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Madden ultimately agrees to put his name and playbook behind EA, he and Davis make the Hall Of Fame — where Madden believes the busts talk to each other at night — and the rest is history. 
 While there are a few brief, tender and heartfelt moments, if director David O. Russell wanted the movie to be a serious, award-winning holiday movie, he failed spectacularly. "Madden" doesn't take itself seriously, and neither should you. The movie will be far more enjoyable to watch if football fans first lower their expectations.
